title: A MALE SLAVE COULD WALK FREE—WHILE HIS WIFE AND CHILDREN STAYED BEHIND
paragraphs: A MALE SLAVE COULD WALK FREE—WHILE HIS WIFE AND CHILDREN STAYED BEHIND
One of the Most Disturbing Laws in Exodus Contains a Sentence About Love, Freedom, and Bondage That Christians Should Not Rush Past
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame.
There are verses people turn into captions, sermons, coffee mugs, and morning devotionals.
And then there are verses like Exodus 21:2–6.
Verses we would rather somebody not bring up.
Because once you actually read them, the questions come fast.
Slaves?
Buying people?
A man becoming free while his wife and children remain behind?
An ear pierced with an awl?
Service for life?
And this is in the Bible?
Yes.
So don't run from the question.
Don't pretend the Hebrew says something softer than it does.
Don't defend God with an explanation Scripture itself never gives.
And don't let somebody rip six verses from an ancient legal world, hold them up without context, and convince you that there is nothing more to understand.
Stay with the text.
Because sometimes faith grows not when we avoid the passages that disturb us, but when we become willing to sit before God long enough to ask:
“Lord… what am I actually reading?”
The Hebrew begins:
כִּי תִקְנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי
Ki tiqneh ‘eved ‘ivri…
“If you acquire a Hebrew servant/slave…”
The important noun is עֶבֶד — ‘eved.
Depending upon context, the word can refer to a servant or slave. We should not automatically erase the harsher English word merely because it makes modern readers uncomfortable.
Then comes the limitation:
שֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים יַעֲבֹד
Shesh shanim ya‘avod…
“Six years he shall serve…”
And then:
וּבַשְּׁבִעִת יֵצֵא לַחָפְשִׁי חִנָּם
Uvashevi‘it yetse lachofshi chinnam.
“And in the seventh he shall go out free, without payment.”
That matters.
The Israelite servant described here could not simply be held indefinitely at the master's discretion. After six years of service, the law required release in the seventh.
But then the passage becomes harder.
If he entered the arrangement already married, his wife went out with him.
But if his master had given him a wife during his service, and she bore children, Exodus 21:4 says that the wife and children remained with the master while the man went out alone.
Read that again.
Don't sanitize it.
Don't pretend it isn't there.
The text really says it.
But notice something many viral attacks on this passage leave out.
Exodus does not say that every Hebrew man's wife and children could simply be seized when he became free.
Verse 3 explicitly says that if he came into the arrangement with a wife, she left with him.
The painful scenario of verse 4 concerns the different case in which the master supplied the wife during the man's period of service.
That distinction does not make the situation emotionally comfortable.
It does make our description of Scripture accurate.
And biblical faithfulness demands both.
We should neither exaggerate the text to make God look monstrous nor dilute the text to make ourselves feel comfortable.
Then comes the sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire passage.
The servant is standing before freedom.
Six years are behind him.
The door is open.
He can leave.
But behind him are people he loves.
And Scripture says:
אָהַבְתִּי אֶת־אֲדֹנִי אֶת־אִשְׁתִּי וְאֶת־בָּנָי
Ahavti et-adoni, et-ishti, ve'et-banai.
“I love my master, my wife, and my children.”
Then:
לֹא אֵצֵא חָפְשִׁי
Lo etse chofshi.
“I will not go out free.”
What a sentence.
“I will not go out free.”
He could walk through the door.
He could leave the household.
He could possess the freedom legally available to him.
But leaving would mean leaving people he loved.
So he stays.
Not because freedom has suddenly become worthless.
Because love has become costly.

His master then brings him before God/the judges—the Hebrew expression אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים (el-ha'elohim) has been understood in these ways in translations and interpretation—and takes him to the door or doorpost.
His ear is pierced with an awl.
And the text says:
וַעֲבָדוֹ לְעֹלָם
Va‘avado le‘olam.
“He shall serve him permanently/for life.”
That is the text.
Now we have to resist a temptation.
It would make a beautiful sermon to jump immediately from that pierced servant to Jesus and announce that Exodus 21:6 is a direct prophecy of Christ.
But Scripture does not call Exodus 21:6 a Messianic prophecy.
So we shouldn't either.
Jesus deserves better than clever connections we cannot prove.
Yet there is a larger biblical story here that eventually leads us somewhere breathtaking.
Because the Bible does not end in Exodus 21.
Israel's laws exist inside the story of a people who themselves had just been delivered from slavery in Egypt.
They knew what oppression tasted like.
They knew what forced labor felt like.
They knew what it meant to cry beneath another man's power.
And as biblical revelation unfolds, the treatment of Israelite servants is further addressed.
Deuteronomy 15:12–15 returns to the six-year servant and commands that when the servant is released, the master must not send that person away empty-handed.
They were to supply the departing servant generously.
Why?
Because God makes Israel remember:
You were slaves in Egypt.
And the LORD redeemed you.
Memory was supposed to produce mercy.
Redemption was supposed to reshape how redeemed people treated vulnerable people.
And that should make every Christian uncomfortable in exactly the right way.
Because it is possible to celebrate being rescued while treating somebody else mercilessly.
It is possible to sing about grace while withholding grace.
It is possible to thank Jesus for forgiving your debt while keeping a detailed emotional ledger of everybody else's.
It is possible to shout about freedom on Sunday and spend Monday enslaved to bitterness.
Maybe that is where this ancient doorway suddenly becomes uncomfortably close.
Because you have doors too.
Maybe nobody has ever pierced your ear against a wooden doorpost.
But something has marked you.
A relationship.
A betrayal.
An addiction.
Pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
Alcohol you insist you control.
Money you cannot stop worshiping.
Approval you cannot stop chasing.
A secret conversation your spouse knows nothing about.
Anger you renamed “discernment.”
Pride you renamed “standards.”
Greed you renamed “ambition.”
Lust you renamed “loneliness.”
Unforgiveness you renamed “boundaries.”
A double life you renamed “struggling.”
And perhaps the most terrifying bondage is the bondage you have learned to call normal.
That is why the Gospel is more than religious inspiration.
Jesus did not come merely to make enslaved people feel better about their chains.
He came to save sinners.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.”
And then He said:
“If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
That is John 8:34–36.
Now the ancient law begins to make us ask a much more personal question.
Not merely:
“How could a servant remain in bondage?”
But:
What keeps me returning to mine?
Some chains are made of iron.
Others are made of memories.
Some prisons have guards.
Others have passwords.
Some masters shout.
Others whisper from a phone screen at 2:13 in the morning:
“One more time.”
Some bondage looks like bondage.
Other bondage wears expensive clothes, attends church, raises its hands during worship, knows Christian vocabulary, and has become very skilled at saying:
“I'm fine.”
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Because perhaps your greatest problem isn't that God refuses to open the door.
Perhaps Christ has been calling you toward repentance, confession, forgiveness, healing, obedience, and freedom…
and part of you keeps looking backward.
Jesus offers something no human master could ever offer.
Not merely release from an earthly contract.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new Master whose lordship does not destroy our humanity but restores it.
And here Christianity becomes gloriously strange.
The apostles can speak of themselves as servants of Christ while simultaneously proclaiming freedom in Christ.
Paul can call himself a δοῦλος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ — doulos Christou Iēsou — a servant/slave of Christ Jesus.
Why?
Because freedom in the Gospel is not autonomous existence where nobody has any claim upon us.
Biblical freedom is liberation from the tyranny of sin so that we may belong to the One for whom we were created.
Sin says:
“Serve me and I will satisfy you.”
Then it consumes you.
Jesus says:
“Come to Me.”
And gives Himself for you.
Sin promises life and pays death.
Christ entered death and gives life.
Sin takes.
Jesus gives Himself.
And this is where we must be careful again.
Jesus was not the Hebrew slave of Exodus 21.
The passage does not say He was.
But when the whole biblical story reaches the cross, we encounter something far greater than the ancient case law itself:
the Lord who voluntarily humbled Himself for those He loved.
Philippians 2 says Christ Jesus took the μορφὴν δούλου — morphēn doulou — “the form of a servant,” humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
He did not cling to privilege while humanity perished.
He came down.
He served.
He suffered.
He was wounded.
He died.
And He rose.
Not because sinners deserved Him.
Because grace is scandalous.
Think about that.
The guilty did not climb their way to the Holy One.
The Holy One came for the guilty.
The Shepherd went after sheep.
The Physician came for the sick.
The Savior came for sinners.
The sinless One carried sin's judgment.
The King wore thorns.
The Lord washed feet.
The Author of life entered death.
And the grave discovered that it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
That is the Gospel.
Not “be a better person.”
Not “try harder.”
Not “hide your scandal well enough that church people never discover it.”
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the story of respectable people impressing God.
It is the story of sinners who could never rescue themselves being rescued by Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been carrying something for years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you're strong.
Maybe your Facebook page looks happy.
Maybe your family thinks you're okay.
Maybe you know exactly when to say “Praise God.”
Maybe you know exactly how to look Christian.
But when the room gets quiet…
you know where the chain is.
Jesus knows too.
And He still calls you.
Not toward comfortable concealment.
Toward the light.
Toward repentance.
Toward grace.
Toward Himself.
You do not have to comment your darkest secret publicly.
But don't lie to God about it.
Sometimes another wounded believer needs to discover that he is not the only person still fighting.
Sometimes your three words become somebody else's reason to pray tonight.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you assume you know their secret sins.
Come back when the chain starts whispering again.
It doesn't.
Not because giving purchases salvation.
It never could.
They cannot.
And we will never tell you that God loves you more because you paid us.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace has no checkout page.

But Scripture does teach voluntary, willing generosity toward Gospel work. Paul speaks of supporting those who proclaim the Gospel, and he also insists that giving must not be “reluctantly or under compulsion,” because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
If you want to glorify God through your resources, do it first by surrendering those resources to His lordship. Then give wherever you are biblically persuaded He is calling you to give.
And if Gospel Warrior is one of those places, we would be deeply grateful to have you standing with us.
But the discount is not the heart of this invitation.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
People are.
Souls matter.
Follow.
Pray.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be content we quietly consume.
The Gospel is news.
News travels.
And somebody in your circle may be smiling publicly while privately wondering whether Jesus could possibly want someone with a story like theirs.
Tell them.
Tell them about Peter after denial.
Tell them about Paul after persecution.
Tell them about the thief beside Jesus.
Tell them about yourself if grace has rewritten you.
Tell them there is repentance.
Tell them there is forgiveness.
Tell them there is a cross.
Tell them there is an empty tomb.
Tell them Jesus still saves sinners.
Exodus 21 began with a disturbing picture:
A man could reach freedom while facing the possibility of leaving people he loved behind.
But Scripture's great story carries us toward a far greater doorway.
Jesus says:
“I am the door.”
And when the Son sets a sinner free, that sinner is free indeed.
So maybe the question you need to carry away from Exodus 21 isn't merely:
“Why would that servant refuse to walk away?”
Maybe tonight the question is:
If Jesus has opened the door, what chain are you still refusing to leave behind?
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Come home.
Because your scandal may explain where you've been…
but it does not have the authority to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus.
The chain remembers who you were. The scars of Christ announce whose you can become.
